blocks.text: This is the same kit as Words into Algebra, with the same five examples, slips, routes and pause, re-made for one learner. Nova is 15 and lives for space. Every sentence now comes from her world, and this page tells you how to meet her there.

blocks.title: Who Nova is
blocks.body: Nova follows launches, saves telescope images, and knows words like orbit, payload and splashdown better than most adults. Don't explain space to her: let her correct you. She will trust the maths faster if it speaks her language, and she will switch off fast if it talks down to her.

blocks.title: The real-world hook (checked)
blocks.body: In April 2026, Artemis II flew four astronauts around the Moon and back in a little over nine days, farther from Earth than any people had travelled before. Christina Koch became the first woman, and Jeremy Hansen the first Canadian, to travel around the Moon. If Nova brings it up, let her tell you about it before you start. That is her lead, and it costs nothing.

blocks.title: Pick your route before you start
blocks.body: Same three routes as the base kit. Each is complete on its own and ends with the next-time note.

items: Quick route: the translation strip together, Example 1 (the docking module), then the quiz until Nova gets three right in a row. Make the note.
Standard route: the Quick route, then Example 2 (the balance) and Example 3 (meteor counts), then Build the equation.
Deep route: all five examples, Words to symbols, Solve it in order, the full quiz, and Nova's own mission problem at the end.

blocks.title: Let her run mission control
blocks.body: On the balance and the docking module, Nova calls each move as a go or no-go before she presses it: "Go: take one patch off both sides." It turns the pause into her voice, and it is exactly the explaining the kit is built around.

blocks.title: The translation strip (keep this in view)
blocks.body: more than, altogether, in total: add. less than, fewer than, difference: take away, and watch the order: 5 less than x is x - 5, never 5 - x. times, twice, each: multiply. shared equally, half of, divided by: divide. is, makes, costs the same as: the equals sign.

blocks.text: Nova is 15, working at O-level standard. She can solve an equation like 3x + 4 = 19 when it is already written down, expand a simple bracket, and work with negatives.

Sentences are where it breaks. The words come in an order that is not the order of the algebra ("5 less than x"), a bracket hides inside a phrase ("twice the sum of"), and a sentence often describes the same thing twice ("together", "the same as"). This kit takes those three traps one at a time.

Her interest is real and current, so the sentences use things she actually cares about: telescope photos, meteor nights, mission patches, a planetarium trip. The real-mission facts sit on this page, not in her questions, so nothing she answers depends on news she might not have seen.

blocks.title: The pause is the method
blocks.body: Before each example, Nova reads the sentence and says it back in plain words: what is unknown, and what is the same as what. Then you wait. The silence feels long, and it is where the understanding happens. If you are short of time, cut an example, not the pause.

blocks.do: Example 1, the docking module (number machine). Nova says the sentence back, then runs the module backwards with the Undo buttons, calling each undo as a go.
blocks.say: Tell me in your own words what we don't know. Then: if we undo the machine, what comes off first?
blocks.why: Undoing the last step first is the whole idea of solving. The machine makes the order visible. Short of time: this example alone carries the Quick route.

blocks.do: Example 2, the balance. Nova takes the same thing off both sides until one mission patch is on its own.
blocks.say: What is the same as what in this sentence? Show me on the scale.
blocks.why: "Costs the same as" is the equals sign. The balance never tips, so Nova sees that every move must happen to both sides. If stuck: let Nova press the buttons and narrate each one.

blocks.do: Example 3, meteor counts. Nova names the three nights in terms of the first before writing anything.
blocks.say: If the first night is n meteors, what are the next two nights?
blocks.why: Consecutive means add 1 each time, not double. The bar model shows the extra 1 and 2 sitting on top of three equal bars. Short of time: skip to the quiz.

blocks.do: Example 4, the launch-pad safety zone: geometry and algebra together. Nova sketches the rectangle and labels all four sides.
blocks.say: How many sides does a perimeter go round? Label every one before you add.
blocks.why: The classic slip is counting each side once. Four labelled sides on a sketch prevent it, and the bar model shows the two extra 30s.

blocks.do: Example 5, the planetarium tickets. Nova groups one ticket with its fee before multiplying.
blocks.say: What does one person pay altogether? Now how many people?
blocks.why: This is where brackets come from: the 4 multiplies the whole of (x + 3). The tiles show the four groups, then open them out.

blocks.title: What only you can do
items: Read Nova's face during the pause and know whether the silence is thinking or being stuck.
Wait a few seconds longer than feels comfortable before you help.
Praise the sentence she says back, not just the right answer.
Ask about the mission she is following, and mean it. Her interest is the engine of this session.
Decide when to stop: end on something Nova got right.

blocks.title: Nova sets you a mission problem
blocks.body: At the end, Nova knows more about space than any worksheet. Ask her to make up a sentence about a real mission, launch or telescope, and you turn it into an equation out loud while she checks you. Get one wrong on purpose and let her catch it.
blocks.prompt: You've done five of mine. Give me a mission problem of yours, and I'll write the equation. You're flight director: tell me go or no-go.

blocks.if: Nova writes 5 - x for "5 less than x"
blocks.then: Ask: which one is getting smaller? x is. So x comes first and 5 is taken from it: x - 5. Try "5 less than 20" with numbers first: 15, so 20 - 5.

blocks.if: Nova writes 2x + 3 for "twice the sum of x and 3"
blocks.then: Ask: what is being doubled, x, or the sum? The sum, so the sum is grouped first: 2(x + 3). Brackets are the word "sum" (or "each") made visible.

blocks.if: Nova writes x, 2x, 3x for consecutive numbers
blocks.then: Say three real nights in a row: 8, 9, 10 meteors. Is 10 three times 8? Each night is one more, so n, n + 1, n + 2.

blocks.if: Nova adds only two sides for a perimeter
blocks.then: Draw the safety zone and walk a finger round the fence. Four sides, two of each length: 2w + 2(w + 30).

blocks.if: Nova writes only half the sentence ("t + 6 = 30")
blocks.then: Ask: who does the 30 belong to, Nova or both of them? "Together" means both, so both go on the left.

blocks.if: Nova goes quiet and stops writing
blocks.then: Open the matching scene and let Nova press the buttons. Moving something is often easier than writing it.

blocks.q: What if Nova can already do all five?
blocks.a: Go straight to her mission problem: Nova writes sentences for you. Writing a sentence from an equation is the same skill in reverse, and harder.

more.q: And if that is easy too?
more.a: Ask for a sentence that needs two unknowns, and stop there. That is the doorway to simultaneous equations, a good place to start next time.

more.q: Do I need to teach simultaneous equations now?
more.a: No. Note it in the next-time note; the next session is built from that.

blocks.q: What if time runs out mid-example?
blocks.a: Stop at the end of the pause, not in the middle of writing. Make the note: it records how far Nova got, so the next session starts there.

more.q: Should I finish the example for Nova?
more.a: No. An unfinished example Nova explained is worth more than a finished one you wrote. Leave it as the first thing next time.

blocks.title: This is an Edition
blocks.body: Words into Algebra is the base kit: football and a made-up learner called Sam, built for any learner. Nova's Edition keeps every mechanic, slip, route and scene and changes only the world, the words and these notes. That is the point: nothing rebuilt, everything re-aimed. Make one for your own learner with the line below.

blocks.title: To rebuild this for another learner
blocks.text: Build an Edition of the MetaDAX Words into Algebra kit for my learner. Keep the five worked examples, the scenes, the games, the six named slips, the three routes and the say-it-back pause. Re-make every sentence and the tutor notes for this learner: [age], loves [their interest], and [one thing about how they learn].
Tick what happened, add a line in your own words, and make the note. It already knows how the games went. Paste it in next time and the next session is built from it.

blocks.title: How did it go?
items: Nova said each sentence back before writing
Nova set me a mission problem

blocks.title: You are mission control
blocks.body: You know more about space than this page does. Every problem here comes from your world. At the end you will make up a mission problem of your own, and your tutor turns it into algebra. Your job is to call go or no-go.
blocks.prompt: Think of one now: a launch, a telescope image, a night of meteors.

blocks.text: Algebra is just a sentence written in signs. x is the number we don't know yet. Before every example, say the sentence back in your own words. Take your time: flight directors don't rush a go.

blocks.title: Words to symbols
blocks.intro: Put each phrase in the box for the sign it means.

items.why: Altogether means add the parts up.
5 less than x is x - 5. Watch the order.
Two sides that cost the same are equal.

blocks.text: Say it back first: what don't we know, and what does the module do to it?

blocks.title: Example 1: the docking module
blocks.ask_learner: Nova doubles the number of Moon photos she saved last night, then adds 5 from the archive. Now she has 23. How many did she save last night? Undo the module to find out.
blocks.why: 2x + 5 = 23. Undo the + 5 first: 2x = 18. Then undo the doubling: x = 9.

blocks.text: Say it back first: what is the same as what?

blocks.title: Example 2: the balance
blocks.ask_learner: Two mission patches and a 4 pound star map cost the same as one patch and an 11 pound telescope filter. How many pounds is one patch?
blocks.why: 2x + 4 = x + 11. Take one patch off both sides: x + 4 = 11. Take 4 off both sides: x = 7.

blocks.text: Say it back first: if the first night is n, what are the other two?

blocks.title: Example 3: meteor nights
blocks.ask_learner: Three nights in a row, Nova counts meteors. Each night she sees one more than the night before. She counts 72 altogether. How many on the first night?

blocks.text: Say it back first: how many sides does the fence go round?

blocks.title: Example 4: the launch-pad safety zone
blocks.ask_learner: A rectangular safety zone around a launch pad is 30 m longer than it is wide. The fence around it is 340 m long. How many metres wide is the zone?

blocks.text: Say it back first: what does one person pay altogether?

blocks.title: Example 5: planetarium tickets
blocks.ask_learner: Each planetarium ticket costs x pounds plus a 3 pound booking fee. Four tickets cost 56 pounds. What is x?
blocks.why: 4(x + 3) = 56. Open the brackets: 4x + 12 = 56. Take 12 away: 4x = 44. Share by 4: x = 11.

blocks.title: Build the equation
blocks.intro: Five friends each pay x pounds for a planetarium ticket and 2 pounds for a star map. Together they pay 70 pounds.

parts.label: What does one person pay?
parts.hint: A ticket and a star map, grouped.

blocks.explain: 5(x + 2) = 70. Share by 5: x + 2 = 14, so a ticket is 12 pounds.

blocks.title: Solve it in order
blocks.intro: Solve 3x + 7 = x + 19 the balance way: the same move to both sides each time.

mistakes.add-x: added x to both sides instead of taking it away
mistakes.take-2: took 2 away instead of sharing by 2

steps.label: Step 1
steps.prompt: Get the x's on one side.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.prompt: Get the numbers on the other side.

blocks.title: Say it in algebra, mission edition
blocks.intro: Read the sentence, say it back to yourself, then pick the algebra that says the same thing.

reversed.name: put the two parts in the wrong order
reversed.guide: Wrote 5 - x for "5 less than x", or 5 / c for "c shared between 5". The words come in the opposite order to the algebra.

bracket.name: left out or misplaced the brackets
bracket.guide: Wrote 2x + 3 for "twice the sum of x and 3". The multiplier belongs to the whole group.

multiples.name: wrote consecutive numbers as multiples
multiples.guide: Wrote n, 2n, 3n instead of n, n + 1, n + 2.

once.name: counted each side of the perimeter once
once.guide: Added one width and one length instead of all four sides.

half.name: wrote only part of the sentence
half.guide: Turned one clause into algebra and dropped the rest, for example the "together".

wrongop.name: used the wrong operation for the words
wrongop.guide: Read "shared", "times" or "of" as the wrong sign.

items.q: 8 fewer than the number of craters Nova counted, c

choices.msg: That one put the two parts in the wrong order. c is the one getting smaller, so c comes first.
Yes. c, with 8 taken away.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. "Fewer than" takes away.

items.q: Three times the hours, h, she spent at the telescope, then 4 more

choices.msg: That one left out or misplaced the brackets. The 4 is added after the tripling, so no bracket.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. "Times" multiplies.
Yes. Triple first, then add 4.

items.hint: What happens first, the tripling or the adding?
items.explain: Three times h is 3h; 4 more makes 3h + 4.

items.q: A telescope costing t pounds, shared equally between 5 friends

choices.msg: Yes. Shared equally means divide.
That one put the two parts in the wrong order. The price is what gets shared, so t is on top.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. Shared equally divides.

items.hint: What is being shared, and into how many parts?

items.q: Half of the photos, p, then 6 fewer

choices.msg: Yes. Halve first, then take 6.
That one put the two parts in the wrong order. The half is getting smaller, so it comes first.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. "Half of" divides by 2.

items.explain: Half of p is p/2; 6 fewer is p/2 - 6.

items.q: Nova logged 6 more satellite passes than her brother. Together they logged 30. Her brother logged b.

choices.msg: That one wrote only part of the sentence. "Together" means both of them.
Yes. Brother b, Nova b + 6, together 30.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. "More than" adds.

items.q: Twice the sum of a number x and 3 is 26.

choices.msg: That one left out or misplaced the brackets. The whole sum is doubled.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. "Twice" multiplies.
Yes. The sum is grouped, then doubled.

items.q: Three planetarium seats in a row have numbers that add up to 45. The smallest is n.

choices.msg: That one wrote consecutive numbers as multiples. Each is one more, not double.
Yes. One more each time.
That one wrote only part of the sentence. The +1 and +2 went missing.

items.hint: Say three real seat numbers in a row first.

items.q: A small solar panel is 1 m wider than it is tall. Its perimeter is 10 m. The height is h.

choices.msg: That one counted each side of the perimeter once. A panel has four sides.
That one left out or misplaced the brackets. Both widths are h + 1.
Yes. Two heights, two widths.

items.explain: 4h + 2 = 10, so h = 2: the panel is 2 m tall and 3 m wide.

items.q: In a rocketry contest, Nova's team scored 5 fewer points than twice its rival's points, a. Nova's team scored 31.

choices.msg: Yes. Twice a, then 5 fewer.
That one put the two parts in the wrong order. Twice a is what gets smaller.
That one left out or misplaced the brackets. The 5 comes off after doubling.

items.q: A model rocket kit costs x pounds. Three kits cost the same as one kit and 40 pounds.

choices.msg: That one wrote only part of the sentence. The one kit on the other side went missing.
Yes. "The same as" is the equals sign.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. Three kits is 3 times x.

items.hint: What is the same as what?

items.q: Four planetarium memberships at k pounds each, less a 20 pound discount, cost 360 pounds.

choices.msg: That one put the two parts in the wrong order. The memberships are what get the discount.
That one left out or misplaced the brackets. The discount is once, not on each membership.
Yes. Four memberships, then 20 off once.

items.hint: Is the discount on each membership, or once?

items.q: f people at a launch watch party share equally into 3 buses. Then 12 more get on one bus, which now has 50.

choices.msg: Yes. Share first, then 12 more on one coach.
That one left out or misplaced the brackets. The 12 join after the sharing.
That one used the wrong operation for the words. Shared equally divides.

blocks.q: What if I can't see where to start?
blocks.a: Say the sentence back and find the word for equals: is, makes, the same as. Everything before it goes on one side.

more.a: Try it with a real number first. If x were 10, what would the sentence say? Then swap the 10 back for x.

more.q: What if I get it wrong?
more.a: Good. The page tells you which slip it was, so you know exactly what to fix next time.

blocks.text: Make up one problem about a mission, a launch or a night under the stars, with a number you don't know. Say it to your tutor. They write the equation, and you call go or no-go.
